c0_01: 1206. / Genghis Khan had taken the warring clans of the steppe / and finally made them one.
c0_02: But to the south, / the huge Jin Empire held what is now northern China.
c0_03: Against its high walls and vast armies, / the Mongols, who had only ever fought on open grass, had barely attacked a single city.
c0_04: So how, / did Genghis Khan get ready for a war with the Jin?
c1_01: When the Mongols first came together, / they had some very old, very rich neighbors.
c1_02: The Jin, founded by the Jurchen people. / The Song, pushed by the Jin down to the Yangtze and beyond.
c1_03: The Western Liao, set up by royals who got out when the Khitan Liao dynasty fell. / And on the Silk Road, the Tangut kingdom of Western Xia.
c1_04: Of all of them, Genghis Khan marked one as a future enemy. The Jin.
c1_05: The biggest reason? / The Jin held the upper hand in trade with the Mongols.
c1_06: So why would that / make someone your enemy?
c1_07: Nomads don't settle down. They follow their herds across the steppe.
c1_08: Which means no farms and no mines. Grain, salt and tea, / plus silk and iron for war, almost all of it had to be traded for.
c1_09: And you traded with settled farming states. / For the Mongols, that meant the Jin, who held all of northern China.
c1_10: If those goods stopped coming in bulk, / life on the steppe only got harder, / and building a great empire was next to impossible.
c1_11: To keep them coming, you had three options. / Stay friendly and trade on a schedule. / Use force and squeeze the grain out of them. / Or take the land and grow it yourself.
c1_12: But right up until Genghis built his empire, / the Jin had worked to block any unity on the steppe, setting tribe against tribe.
c1_13: Now every tribe stood together. / So how long before the Jin cut the trade routes just to weaken him?
c1_14: From where Genghis stood, the choice was simple. / Bring down the Jin, or live at their mercy.
c2_01: There was one problem. Genghis had spent his life fighting on open grassland, / and he'd never really gone up against a settled state. / Attacking an empire that size right away was out of the question.
c2_02: So he looked to another settled kingdom on the Silk Road. / Western Xia.
c2_03: The Tangut founded Western Xia in 1038, / and it grew rich as a middleman on the Silk Road. / At its peak, it was strong enough to make the Song Dynasty pay it off every year.
c2_05: By now Xia still had around 150,000 troops and plenty of fortresses, / but its ruling families kept fighting each other, and the state was shaky.
c2_06: That made it the perfect dress rehearsal for the Jin.
c2_07: And Xia was close with the Jin, / so before going after the Jin, Genghis had to secure his back.
c2_08: He'd actually tested Xia once already, in 1205, / just before he united the steppe.
c2_09: His excuse was that Xia had taken in Senggum, a runaway Kereit prince. / And that raid put him in front of a town built by settled people for the very first time.
c2_10: It was only a small frontier fort. / Arrows came flying from behind a wall, which threw the Mongols completely, / but they surrounded the place and took it.
c2_11: They wrecked the town, looted the Xia heartland, / and rode home.
c2_12: The fallout came a year later. / Blamed for failing to stop the Mongols, / the emperor was overthrown by his own cousin.
c3_01: Genghis came back for real / a year after he became Great Khan.
c3_02: Up to 1209 the Mongols invaded Xia again and again, / trying whatever they could think of to crack its fortresses.
c3_03: First, they drove prisoners ahead of them. / Their bodies filled the moat in front of the walls, / and on top of that they worked as shields against the archers above.
c3_04: Drawing a bow over and over is brutal work. / And now those archers were shooting their own people, / so the men on the walls wore down, in body and in mind.
c3_05: The Mongols also burned and looted the villages around a fortress on purpose. / They tried not to kill the people there, and pushed them toward the walls instead.
c3_06: Suddenly the city had far more mouths to feed, and supplies drained away. / Order broke down, / and the mood inside dragged down the garrison's morale.
c3_07: At Zhongxing, the Xia capital, / they tried something reckless. A siege by water.
c3_08: The Yellow River ran right past Zhongxing, / so they dammed it and bent the current toward the walls.
c3_09: And they did move the river. / But these men had spent their whole lives on the steppe, and nobody had done the math.
c3_10: The water burst into the Mongol camp, / and the attackers took the worst of it.
c3_11: Even so, once the water drained, the Mongols closed around the city again.
c3_12: Desperate, Xia begged the Jin for help. / The Jin refused. Their enemies fighting each other was good news.
c3_13: With no help coming, in 1209 the emperor of Xia surrendered, and Xia became a Mongol vassal.
c3_14: The Mongols got grain, / and the emperor's daughter as well.
c4_01: For years, the Jin had kept the steppe divided. / The last thing they wanted was a new power rising up there.
c4_02: Whenever one tribe got strong, they backed its rivals, / switching their support between the Tatars, the Kereit, the Naiman and others.
c4_03: Keep them fighting, and they'd wear each other out.
c4_04: But why were the Jin so paranoid about nomads?
c4_05: This was a seriously powerful state. / The Jurchen grew up on horseback and were deadly in open battle, / and the pride of their army was the Iron Pagoda, their heavy cavalry.
c4_06: They'd destroyed the Liao, / and driven the Song out of the north, taking half of China's heartland.
c4_07: And that's exactly why they were scared. / They knew another rising power from the steppe could do the same thing to them.
c4_08: They weren't the first to worry about it. / The Sui, the Tang and the Liao, all with nomad roots, had felt the same way.
c4_09: That's how strong the steppe peoples were.
c4_10: So when Genghis united the steppe in 1206, / the Jin saw the danger and started to prepare.
c4_11: But then Zhangzong died with no heir, / and the crown went to his indecisive, incompetent uncle, Wanyan Yongji, the Prince of Wei.
c4_12: He sent envoys to remind Genghis who served whom.
c5_01: Word came that an imperial decree was on its way, / so Genghis went to Jingzhou, on Jin territory.
c5_02: The envoy arrived, / and told him to kneel and receive the decree.
c5_03: Genghis asked who the new emperor was, / and the envoy answered: the Prince of Wei.
c5_04: Genghis couldn't believe it. He was furious. / He turned to face south, and he spat.
c5_05: Then he said it out loud. / "I thought the Son of Heaven was someone Heaven chose. / A weakling like that gets to be emperor? / Why would I bow to him?"
c5_06: These two had history, you see.
c5_07: Genghis used to send tribute every year to the old emperor, Zhangzong. / When the Prince of Wei came to collect it, Genghis refused to bow.
c5_08: The prince was so angry he wanted Genghis dead.
c5_09: Anyway, Genghis rode straight back north. / When the new emperor heard about it, he lost his temper, / and ordered that if Genghis ever came with tribute again, he was to be killed.
c5_10: Then, in case the Mongols attacked, / he started building forts all along the border.
c6_01: Genghis had always seen war with the Jin as unavoidable. / Now he was ready to start it.
c6_02: He called a kurultai, told the tribes they were going to war, / and gave them two reasons.
c6_03: One: the Jin had backed the Tatars, the people who killed his father.
c6_04: Two: the Jin had once captured one of his ancestors in war, / strapped him to a wooden donkey, and nailed him to it.
c6_05: Genghis led a huge army into Jin territory. / And he split it. / His main force headed for the border on the road to the Jin capital, / while his sons drove into the northwest.
c6_06: When the news reached the Jin, / they gave their main army to a general named Wanyan Chengyu.
c6_07: All the food near the border was hauled off to the capital, / so the Mongols would find nothing to eat.
c6_08: The border forts got ready, / and to smash the Mongol main force, / Chengyu massed his army at Yehuling, on the road to Juyong Pass.
c6_09: Genghis sent his most trusted commanders, Jebe among them, to lead the way and hit the fortress of Wushabao.
c6_10: Its commander, Duji Sizhong, was rebuilding it, and the work wasn't done. / His army was smashed in no time, / and Wushabao fell.
c6_11: The Mongol main force came back together, rested, / and turned toward Yehuling.
c6_12: There, the Jin commander was getting ready for the decisive battle.
c6_13: But right before it began, / a man sent from the Jin side stood in front of Genghis Khan.
c6_14: And he started telling him exactly where the Jin army was.
c0_05: The Mongol invasion of the Jin, part one. / Let's begin.
c6_15: The Mongol invasion of the Jin, / continues in part two.
